subtype: Approach: blaming the teacher or the syllabus [Pitfall]
passage: I am Zainab, and I sit two benches from Parul. After the Chemistry test she waved her paper around and said, "The paper was unfair, and Sir cannot teach. Nobody could pass that." Two friends nodded, and for a day Parul looked lighter, almost bright. But I noticed she never opened the Chemistry book that week, not once, and when I asked what she would do differently she shrugged. The next test was on Friday. Same result. She stared at the marks and this time said nothing. I do not know what she believes deep down. I only saw the plan never appear, and the days going by.

qa.q: What did Parul say about the paper?
qa.a: Parul said the paper was unfair and that nobody could pass it.

qa.q: What might Parul have been feeling when she blamed the paper?
qa.a: Hurt and defensive, since blaming protected her pride for a while, though Zainab cannot be sure.

qa.q: What could Parul do to make the next result different?
qa.a: Look at which questions lost marks and ask the teacher or a friend for help with those, because a specific plan works better than blame.

qa.q: How might the teacher see the claim that the paper was unfair?
qa.a: Probably with disappointment, since the paper was the same for everyone, and the teacher may be ready to help if Parul asks.

grounding: A student blames the teacher and paper, which protects self-esteem for a while but produces no plan, so the next result is the same.

subtype: Approach: blaming the teacher or the syllabus [Pitfall]
passage:
October. Elizabeth gets 31 in the Physics unit test. At lunch she tells Jahnavi, "Mr Menon can't teach. And that paper was unfair, half of it wasn't even in the notes." Jahnavi, who got 58, says nothing. By the time the bell rings, Elizabeth feels better.
November. Jahnavi asks if she wants to go through the wrong answers together. "What's the point? He'll just set something weird again." Elizabeth spends the weekend on her English project instead.
December. The second unit test comes back: 33. Elizabeth stares at it. The pre-boards are six weeks away, and she has no list, no plan, nothing to show for two months except a story about Mr Menon. She crumples the paper, then smooths it out again.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth get in the second unit test?
How does Elizabeth seem to feel when she stares at the second result?
qa.a: She seems shaken and worried, realising the blame gave her no plan and the pre-boards are close.

qa.q: What else could Elizabeth have done in November?
qa.a: Accept Jahnavi's offer and go through the wrong answers, since finding her own gaps would give her a plan whatever the teacher is like.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi see Elizabeth's complaints about Mr Menon?
qa.a: Jahnavi, who scored 58 with the same teacher, may quietly doubt the blame, yet still offers help.

grounding: Shows over three months how blaming the teacher and the paper protects a student's feelings but leaves no plan and the same result.

subtype: Approach: blaming the teacher or the syllabus [Pitfall]
passage: Jahnavi mol, blaming your teacher? Sit, let me tell you what your Jomon Uncle did at your age. In pre-degree I failed Chemistry. Twenty-six marks. And I decided it was Thomas Sir's fault: he mumbled, he wrote too fast, the paper was cruel. I told everyone. My friends agreed, and it felt lovely. For two months I told that story and did nothing else. No list of what I got wrong, not one extra hour. Then the second test came. Twenty-eight. Same Sir, same mumbling, and now the final exam was eight weeks off. My friend Babu had the same Sir and got sixty. That night I finally opened my paper and found I didn't understand valency at all. Not Sir's fault. Mine to fix.

qa.q: What did young Jomon score in the second test?
How did young Jomon feel while blaming Thomas Sir?
qa.a: He felt comforted and less ashamed because his friends agreed, which is why the story was so easy to keep telling.

qa.q: Which choice inside the story finally moved things forward?
qa.a: Opening the failed paper to see what went wrong, because it showed the real gap, valency, which could actually be worked on.

qa.q: What would have changed if Jomon had checked the paper after the first test?
qa.a: The valency gap would have shown up two months earlier, with far more time to fix it before the final exam.

grounding: An elder recalls blaming a teacher and the paper for a failed subject, getting the same result with the deadline closer.
